title: How Do You Spend Your Status?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership essay argues that status is a currency leaders can either hoard for personal comfort or spend deliberately on others, and that the best leaders treat it as something meant to circulate rather than accumulate. It contends that every leader carries some measure of status by virtue of results, relationships, title, and reputation, and that the real leadership question is never whether a leader has influence but what they choose to do with it. The piece offers a specific, low-effort practice, identifying one person each week who could use an advocate, an introduction, or public credit, as the mechanism for converting abstract status into concrete acts of generosity. Its central paradox is that spending status on others, rather than depleting a leader's influence, compounds it: leaders remembered most are not those who climbed highest but those who reached back to lift others.
points: The essay's core reframing, status as currency meant to circulate, not a privilege to hoard, turns an abstract concept into an actionable leadership practice.
Its central paradox is that spending status on others compounds rather than depletes it, directly countering the zero-sum assumption that influence is a finite resource to be protected.

The weekly practice it proposes, find one person who needs an advocate, introduction, or public credit, is deliberately small-scale and repeatable rather than aspirational, making the advice usable rather than merely inspirational.
The closing line reframes leadership legacy itself around generosity of influence rather than achievement.
quotes: Leaders who focus only on the personal benefits of status miss a tremendous opportunity to motivate and inspire people. In contrast, the best leaders can't wait to spend their status on others.

Good leaders view their status and influence as a currency meant to circulate, not a privilege to hoard. They spend it deliberately on those around them who need a lift-up, an opportunity to showcase their skills, or a moment to feel special.
The question isn't whether a leader has status. Almost every leader does, in some measure. The question is what they spend it on.
Leaders who want to spend their status well start small. They look for one person each week who could use an advocate, an introduction, or a word of credit in front of others.
Status spent on others doesn't disappear. It compounds. The leader who gives status away generously always ends up with more of it.
The leaders we remember the most aren't the ones who climbed the highest, but the ones who reached back to lift others.
